summary.title: The properties of highly concentrated aqueous CH3COOK/Na binary electrolyte and its use in sodium-ion batteries
summary.authors: Shahid Khalid, Nicolò Pianta, Simone Bonizzoni, Piercarlo Mustarelli, Riccardo Ruffo
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental study (materials characterization + electrochemical proof of concept)
summary.executive_summary: This work investigates highly concentrated aqueous binary electrolytes based on potassium acetate (CH3COOK) combined with varying amounts of sodium acetate (CH3COONa), aiming to develop safe, low-cost, and environmentally friendly electrolytes for aqueous sodium-ion batteries. The motivation stems from the limitations of conventional lithium-ion batteries, which rely on flammable, toxic, and expensive organic electrolytes, and from the narrow thermodynamic electrochemical stability window of water (1.23 V), which can only be kinetically extended to about 1.5 V in dilute solutions. Super-concentrated 'water-in-salt' electrolytes offer a pathway to widen this window by reducing the activity of water molecules through strong ion hydration. While fluorinated salts such as LiTFSI and NaFSI have been widely used, they suffer from toxicity, cost, and availability issues. In contrast, acetate salts like CH3COOK and CH3COONa are cost-effective, highly soluble, and widely available, making them attractive alternatives. The authors prepared four binary electrolytes with a constant CH3COOK concentration of 20 mol kg⁻¹ and varying CH3COONa concentrations of 1, 2.5, 5, and 7 mol kg⁻¹, along with a 1 M NaAc reference solution. They comprehensively characterized these electrolytes using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), rheology, conductivity measurements, and electrochemical techniques. The results show that increasing salt concentration shifts the glass transition temperature to higher values, indicating stronger ion-water interactions and a transition from salt-in-water to water-in-salt behavior. The most concentrated solution, 7N20K (7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc + 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc), exhibited the best compromise between transport properties and electrochemical stability, with a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C and an electrochemical stability window up to 3 V under ideal conditions. As a proof of concept for sodium-ion batteries, a carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (NASICON) electrode demonstrated reversible Na⁺ insertion and de-insertion at about -0.7 V vs. SHE, with a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹, an average charge efficiency of 96% at low current, and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. The low charge transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV highlights the excellent interfacial kinetics. These findings demonstrate the potential of highly concentrated aqueous acetate electrolytes for developing safe and sustainable alkaline-ion rechargeable batteries.

The low charge transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV highlights the excellent interfacial kinetics. These findings demonstrate the potential of highly concentrated aqueous acetate electrolytes for developing safe and sustainable alkaline-ion rechargeable batteries.

Research Context
Super-concentrated aqueous electrolytes are gaining interest for safer, cheaper, and more sustainable battery chemistries. Conventional lithium-ion batteries suffer from safety and cost issues due to flammable and toxic organic electrolytes. The narrow electrochemical stability window of water limits the performance of aqueous electrolytes. High concentration regimes can widen the ESW by reducing water activity through strong ion hydration. Fluorinated salts used in water-in-salt electrolytes face toxicity, cost, and availability challenges. Acetate salts offer cost-effective, highly soluble, and widely available alternatives to fluorinated salts. NASICON materials are promising electrode materials due to their stable structure and large ionic channels.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether highly concentrated aqueous CH3COOK/CH3COONa binary electrolytes can serve as viable water-in-salt electrolytes for sodium-ion batteries. The hypothesis is that increasing CH3COONa concentration will improve the electrochemical stability window while maintaining acceptable transport properties. It is hypothesized that the most concentrated electrolyte will exhibit optimal conductivity and stability for practical battery applications. The authors predict that a carbon-coated NASICON electrode will enable reversible sodium-ion intercalation in the most concentrated electrolyte. The expected outcome is high charge efficiency and good capacity retention over extended cycling.

Methodological Details
Four binary electrolytes were prepared with a constant CH3COOK concentration of 20 mol kg⁻¹ and varying CH3COONa concentrations. A 1 M NaAc solution was prepared as a reference for comparison. NaAc and KAc were sourced from Alfa Aesar with a purity of 99%. High-quality Milli-Q water with a conductivity of 6.7 µS cm⁻¹ was used as the solvent. Electrolytes were prepared by dissolving salts under sonication and stored at room conditions. Carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (CLTP) was synthesized using a one-pot sol-gel route with glucose as the carbon source. The synthesis involved dissolving NH4H2(PO4)3 and Ti(OC4H9)4 in ethanol, followed by stirring at 55°C for 4 hours. CH3COOLi·2H2O (0.52 g) and glucose (0.58 g) were added as lithium and carbon sources. The mixture was heated to 80°C to remove ethanol and form a gel, then dried under vacuum at 100°C. The precursor was calcined at 800°C for 6 hours under argon flux in a tubular furnace. Pristine LiTi2(PO4)3 (LTP) was synthesized via the same route without glucose. XRD analysis was performed using a Rigaku Miniflex 600 with a Cu cathode.

Procedures And Architectures
XRD analysis was performed in a 2θ range from 10° to 80° with a step size of 0.02 and scan speed of 1 deg min⁻¹. SEM imaging was conducted using a Zeiss® Gemini SEM 450. Viscosity measurements were performed using an MCR Rheometer 102 with a parallel plate setup. Shear tests were conducted with shear rates ranging from 10 to 300 s⁻¹ at temperatures of 10, 20, 30, and 40°C. Thermal analysis was performed using DSC with a temperature range from -120°C to 90°C. The DSC protocol involved cooling from 30°C to -120°C at 1°C min⁻¹, followed by a 5-minute isotherm and heating to 90°C. Conductivity measurements were performed using EIS with a dip probe cell with two platinum foils. Impedance spectra were recorded in a frequency range of 1 Hz to 200 kHz with an amplitude of 25 mV. Electrochemical measurements were conducted in flooded three-electrode cells with glassy carbon, platinum mesh, and double junction SCE. GCPL measurements were conducted at different current rates, starting with 10 cycles at 0.1C and increasing to 0.5C, 1C, 5C, and 10C. In the C-rate calculation, 1C corresponds to 136 mA g⁻¹, considering the insertion and de-insertion of two alkaline ions. Electrodes were prepared by dip-coating carbon cloth current collectors in slurries of active materials.

Key Results
The glass transition temperature (Tg) increases with increasing salt concentration, indicating stronger ion-water interactions. The most concentrated solution, 7N20K, exhibited a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C. The 7N20K electrolyte showed an electrochemical stability window up to 3 V under ideal conditions. The 7N20K electrolyte exhibited the best compromise between transport properties and electrochemical stability. The carbon-coated NASICON electrode demonstrated reversible Na⁺ insertion and de-insertion at about -0.7 V vs. SHE. The first-cycle anodic capacity was 85 mAh g⁻¹ with an average charge efficiency of 96% at low current. The capacity retention after 60 cycles was 90%. The low charge transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV highlights the excellent interfacial kinetics. The diffusion coefficient at room temperature was around 10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹. The 7N20K electrolyte outperformed the diluted solution in terms of specific capacity and efficiency.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The increase in Tg with concentration indicates a transition from salt-in-water to water-in-salt behavior. The reduced water activity at high concentration suppresses hydrogen evolution and widens the ESW. The low charge transfer activation energy suggests excellent interfacial kinetics for sodium-ion intercalation. The aqueous electrolyte improves the diffusion of alkaline ions inside the electrode structure. The results demonstrate the potential of highly concentrated aqueous acetate electrolytes for developing safe and sustainable alkaline-ion rechargeable batteries.

Contradictions And Limitations
The ESW expansion on the anodic side is not as significant as it is on the cathodic side. The LSV procedure may lead to overestimated decomposition limits due to the large amount of electrolyte and quasi-ideal electrocatalytic electrode. The viscosity measurements were limited by instrumental constraints, preventing exploration of the full VTF behavior.
